newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada offers to take U.S. plutonium waste.
newsitem.headline: Canada offers to take U.S. plutonium waste.

text.p: Canadian Environment Minister Sergio Marchi said on Tuesday that Canada would be happy to accept U.S. military plutonium for use in civilian nuclear reactors.

"We think it is a worthwhile project for Canada to help out," Marchi told a news conference. "I'm not sure we're going to take every last ounce of plutonium, but I think Canada is prepared to use its industry, use its technology and use its honest brokery in the international community to the advantage of that community."

He spoke a day after Washington announced a $2 billion project to scrap 50 tons of plutonium left over from the nuclear arms programme by encasing it in glass and burning it as fuel in nuclear power plants.
Also on Tuesday, Marchi introduced legislation to deal with Canada's pollution problems. The legislation contained no provisions on the import of nuclear materials.

Marchi said Canada should accept the highly radioactive plutonium to promote world peace and finance the country's nuclear industry. He said that any project would have to pass environmental assessment before being approved.

Ontario Hydro, the provincial government-owned utility in Canada's most populous province, was considering accepting up to 100 tons of plutonium extracted from U.S. and Russian mothballed nuclear warheads over 25 years, a government spokesman told Reuters.

Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd, a government agency, agreed to burn small amounts of radioactive material in an experimental research reactor at Chalk River, Ontario, early next year, Bob Gadsby, a project director at the agency said.
A similar project to ship U.S. plutonium to Canada was shelved last month after opposition from U.S. anti-nuclear groups.
Burning the deadly plutonium in power plants would reduce plutonium residue by half, but would also produce a more lethal spent fuel than conventional nuclear-reactor waste.
Environmental and anti-nuclear groups voiced concern about the environmental implications and impact on local communities.
"There's no need for Canada to import U.S. waste material, particularly plutonium," Paul Muldoon, a lawyer for the Canadian Environmental Law Association, told a news conference.
